lesson.title: The Brakes on Cell Division: Tumor Suppressor Genes
lesson.summary: Tumor suppressor genes encode proteins that normally restrain the cell cycle or trigger repair and cell death in damaged cells, and cancer typically requires both copies of a tumor suppressor gene to be lost.
lesson.body:
If proto-oncogenes are the accelerator, tumor suppressor genes are the brakes. These genes encode proteins that normally restrain cell division, whether by halting the cell cycle at a checkpoint, forcing damaged cells to repair themselves before continuing, or triggering programmed cell death when damage is too severe to fix. Cancer arises not only from an overactive accelerator but, just as often, from failed brakes.

The protein p53 is one of the best known tumor suppressors and is often called the guardian of the genome. When a cell's DNA damage sensors detect a problem, p53 is activated and enforces the G1 checkpoint: it turns on genes whose protein products inhibit cyclin CDK complexes, most notably a protein called p21, which blocks the activity needed to move the cell into S phase. This buys time for repair enzymes to fix the damage. If the damage is too extensive to repair, p53 can instead push the cell toward apoptosis, programmed cell death, eliminating a cell that would otherwise risk passing mutations to its descendants. Because it sits at the center of this decision, p53 is disabled, by mutation or other means, in a large share of human cancers.

The retinoblastoma protein, Rb, works at the same checkpoint through a different mechanism. In its active form, Rb binds and holds inactive a transcription factor called E2F, which is required to switch on the genes needed to enter S phase. Rb is released from E2F only when it is phosphorylated by cyclin CDK complexes at the appropriate point in G1, directly connecting Rb's control of the checkpoint to the cyclin and CDK activity covered earlier. When Rb is lost or mutated, E2F is left unrestrained, and the cell can slip past the G1 checkpoint without the normal go ahead signal.

A defining feature of tumor suppressor genes is that losing one copy is usually not enough to cause a problem, because the other, normal copy still produces enough functional protein to do the job. Both copies typically have to be lost or inactivated before the brake fails completely, an idea known as the two hit hypothesis. This principle was worked out through studies of retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer. Children who inherit one already mutated copy of the Rb gene from a parent need only a single additional mutation, a second hit, in any retinal cell to lose Rb function entirely, so they tend to develop tumors early and often in both eyes. Children who inherit two normal copies need two independent mutational hits in the same cell, a much rarer event, so sporadic retinoblastoma appears later and usually in only one eye. The same two hit logic applies to other well known tumor suppressors, including the DNA repair genes BRCA1 and BRCA2, where inheriting one already mutated copy substantially raises the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
